# Plan: Stage 3 (changing constellations) + rotating Earth + low-poly Earth + README assumptions

## Context
Stages 1 and 2 are committed (53 tests pass; Pyodide web app with globe, sky plot, Live and Monte Carlo tabs). The user now asks for:
1. A **README that records every modelling assumption** (including the new common-clock one) and logs every later change to an assumption. Standing rule.
2. A **rotating Earth** (so geostationary satellites work), and a **low-poly Earth** that looks like Earth.
3. **Stage 3**: add/remove satellites, orbit visuals for new satellites, GPS/Galileo/BeiDou presets, elliptical orbits allowed, a geostationary toggle, a Walker T/P/F generator, a time-window control and LCM toggle for the Monte Carlo, and time snapping during Monte Carlo runs.

## Decisions made with the user
| Topic | Decision |
|---|---|
| Receiver clock | **One common clock** for all constellations (4 unknowns). Labelled in UI and README. An "estimate inter-system biases" option is a candidate for after Stage 4. |
| Earth | **Rotating** at the sidereal rate. Replaces the nonrotating assumption (recorded in the README change log). |
| Earth look | **Low-poly**: icosphere, ~5,000 flat-shaded triangles; land/ocean from **Natural Earth 110 m land outlines** (public domain, committed to the repo, source in papers.txt) |
| Presets | GPS (Walker 24/6/1, existing), Galileo, **BeiDou MEO** and **BeiDou IGSO+GEO** as separate additive presets (adding both = full BeiDou with no duplicates) |
| Adding satellites | Easy **circular** form (altitude, inclination, RAAN, starting phase) + **elliptical** option + **Walker T/P/F** button + **Geostationary** toggle |
| Removal | **Checkbox per satellite** (off = failed: faint ghost, excluded from visibility, DOP, Monte Carlo), master checkbox per constellation, delete button for added satellites, and **click a satellite on the globe** to toggle it |
| Colours | **By constellation**; orbit rings take the constellation colour |
| Layout | **Third sidebar tab: Live / Monte Carlo / Constellation** |
| Time window | **User-defined, default 365 days**, plus a **toggle for the approximate LCM of the periods**; with it on, the window follows the LCM and updates as satellites change |
| Time snapping | During a run the time controls are locked. Every n-th trial (n = trials/s, about 1 per second) is the **featured trial**: the globe time snaps to its time and the timeline follows. |

## Proposed defaults (to confirm at approval)
- Earth rotation: omega = 2*pi / 86,164.0905 s. At t = 0, longitude 0 points along inertial +x (arbitrary epoch, no real date). Orbits stay in the inertial frame; ground-fixed things (receiver, graticule, trial dots, land mesh) rotate.
- **Monte Carlo is unaffected by rotation.** A trial's longitude and time are drawn independently, so longitude + omega*t is uniform and independent of t; the joint statistics are identical to a nonrotating Earth. Rotation changes the live view, fixed-site time series (Stage 5) and GEO satellites, not Monte Carlo averages. The analytic check still applies.
- Geostationary: a = (mu*(T_sid/2pi)^2)^(1/3) = 42,164.17 km, e = 0, i = 0, phase M0 = longitude (E), computed in code, not hard-coded.

## Decisions made with the user
| Topic | Decision |
|---|---|
| Terrain model | **Conical**: one blocking angle in every direction (the shape is a parameter, so other shapes can come later) |
| Monte Carlo | Same cone at every trial (orientation does not matter for a cone) |
| Visual | **Blocked sight lines drawn in another colour** (red, dashed) on the globe |
| Controls | **Fourth tab "Terrain"** |
| Colours | **Colour picker per group and per satellite** (a satellite's own colour overrides its group's). New groups get **one random bright hue**, chosen away from the existing groups' hues; each new single satellite gets its own random hue; presets keep their fixed colours. A colour chosen in the add form overrides the random one |
| Add screen | **Pop-up with cards, then the form**: GPS, Galileo, BeiDou MEO, BeiDou IGSO+GEO, Single satellite, Geostationary, Walker. Preset cards add directly; custom cards open their form in the dialog. The globe stays visible for the preview |

- **Physics:** a satellite is usable if it is switched on and its elevation is at least the terrain's blocking angle in its direction. For a cone this is a constant, the same as the existing elevation mask. So **A13's analytic check applies unchanged** (already tested at masks of 0, 10 and 30 deg).

- New `web/satmodels.js`: four merged `BufferGeometry` models built from boxes, plates and a low cone (dish), with vertex shading so the wings are a darker shade of the material colour. One material per satellite (colour), and one shared geometry per model.

- The Constellation tab keeps the satellite list plus an **"Add satellites…"** button. The current add-satellite and Walker forms move into a floating dialog over the globe (non-modal, so the globe stays visible).

- Card types: 4 presets (added directly; already present shows "Remove"), Single satellite (circular/elliptical), Geostationary (longitude), Walker T/P/F. Each form has the colour control and the live preview.

1. Terrain: Python + tests, Terrain tab, red blocked lines, README.
2. Colours (pickers, random hues).
3. Satellite models (+ normals).
4. Selection dialog + orbit preview.
5. Full browser regression and README.

  - A cone of angle e gives the same visibility and DOP as a mask of e.

  - Preview output: paths, positions on their rings, normals.
  - Normals are unit vectors, perpendicular to the position, and equal to r x v.
- **Browser (headless Chrome):**

  - The colour pickers change the globe and list colours.
  - New groups get one shared random colour, distinct from the others.
  - The dialog flows: preset adds, custom forms, cancel.
  - The preview appears on edit and hover and clears on close.
  - Models render (screenshots inspected).
  - No JavaScript errors.
  - All earlier suites still pass.

"""Receiver geometry: where a receiver is, and where a satellite appears in its sky.

Earth is a perfect sphere of radius R_EARTH (km) that rotates at the sidereal rate.

Frames: the satellites live in a fixed (inertial) frame with +z through the north
pole and +x toward the vernal equinox (the direction astronomers measure sidereal
time from). The Earth turns about +z, so a receiver at fixed (lat, lon) on the
ground moves through that frame. Latitude/longitude arguments below are always
Earth-fixed (what a map shows).

Time: t is seconds after the epoch, 2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. The angle between
longitude 0 (Greenwich) and +x is the Greenwich Mean Sidereal Time (GMST), so a
calendar date and time fixes where the Earth is turned. (Precession, nutation,
polar motion and the small UTC/UT1 difference are ignored.)

Every function works on a single receiver or on a whole array of receivers
(Monte Carlo trials): extra leading array dimensions are carried through.
"""

import numpy as np

R_EARTH = 6378.137          # km (WGS-84 equatorial radius, used as the sphere radius)
T_SIDEREAL = 86164.0905     # s, one rotation of the Earth relative to the stars
OMEGA_EARTH = 2.0 * np.pi / T_SIDEREAL   # rad/s


def julian_date(year, month, day, hour=0.0):
    """Julian Date of a UTC calendar date (Gregorian calendar), Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, ch. 7."""
    if month <= 2:
        year, month = year - 1, month + 12
    a = year // 100
    b = 2 - a + a // 4
    return int(365.25 * (year + 4716)) + int(30.6001 * (month + 1)) + day + hour / 24.0 + b - 1524.5


def gmst_deg(jd):
    """Greenwich Mean Sidereal Time (degrees, 0-360) at Julian Date jd (UT), Meeus eq. 12.4."""
    T = (jd - 2451545.0) / 36525.0
    theta = 280.46061837 + 360.98564736629 * (jd - 2451545.0) + 0.000387933 * T**2 - T**3 / 38710000.0
    return theta % 360.0


EPOCH_UTC = "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"                 # t = 0
EPOCH_JD = julian_date(2026, 1, 1)                 # 2461041.5
EARTH_ANGLE_AT_EPOCH = gmst_deg(EPOCH_JD)          # degrees, about 100.66 (GMST 6h 42m 39s)


def earth_angle_deg(t):
    """Angle (degrees) from inertial +x to longitude 0 at t seconds after the epoch: the GMST,
    which grows at the sidereal rate (one turn per 86,164.0905 s)."""
    return EARTH_ANGLE_AT_EPOCH + np.degrees(OMEGA_EARTH * np.asarray(t, dtype=float))


def receiver_position(lat_deg, lon_deg, t=0.0):
    """Receiver position (km) in the inertial frame at time t: shape (..., 3)."""
    lat, lon = np.broadcast_arrays(np.radians(lat_deg), np.radians(np.asarray(lon_deg) + earth_angle_deg(t)))
    return R_EARTH * np.stack([np.cos(lat) * np.cos(lon),
                               np.cos(lat) * np.sin(lon),
                               np.sin(lat)], axis=-1)


def enu_basis(lat_deg, lon_deg, t=0.0):
    """Local East, North, Up unit vectors (inertial frame, at time t) as the rows of a
    3x3 matrix: shape (..., 3, 3).

    Multiplying a vector by this matrix gives its (east, north, up) components.
    """
    lat, lon = np.broadcast_arrays(np.radians(lat_deg), np.radians(np.asarray(lon_deg) + earth_angle_deg(t)))
    east = np.stack([-np.sin(lon), np.cos(lon), np.zeros_like(lon)], axis=-1)
    north = np.stack([-np.sin(lat) * np.cos(lon), -np.sin(lat) * np.sin(lon), np.cos(lat)], axis=-1)
    up = np.stack([np.cos(lat) * np.cos(lon), np.cos(lat) * np.sin(lon), np.sin(lat)], axis=-1)
    return np.stack([east, north, up], axis=-2)

      el_deg  : degrees above the local horizontal plane        shape (..., N)

    el = np.degrees(np.arcsin(np.clip(up, -1.0, 1.0)))
    az = np.degrees(np.arctan2(east, north)) % 360.0
    return az, el, unit

Step 1, Stage 4 terrain, is done. The other four steps (colours, models, the Add dialog and the orbit preview) aren't started yet. All 179 Python tests pass and the browser Terrain checks pass 13/13, with no JavaScript errors. Nothing from this round is committed yet.

## What you get

- **Terrain tab:** a new fourth tab with a "Valley / obstacles" switch and a wall angle from 0° to 80° (slider plus number box, default 20°). It includes a small side-view drawing of the cone-shaped valley.
- **Live view:** any satellite below the wall angle is hidden, in every direction. On the globe, sight lines to hidden satellites are **red and dashed**, and usable ones stay green.
- **Monte Carlo:** uses the same valley. The results header shows the angle, and the controls lock during runs like the rest.
- **Tab bar:** I tightened the tab styling so four tabs fit on one line.

A cone is exactly an elevation mask, so the analytic check still applies. In a 20° valley the browser Monte Carlo mean is 5.443 against the analytic 5.457, at −2.5σ. That is inside the 4σ limit, though on the high side. The Python test at the same angle also passes.

## First Stage 4 result (GPS alone, N ≥ 4 and PDOP ≤ 6)

| Valley wall | Mean in view | Availability | Median PDOP |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0° | 9.1 | 100% | 1.5 |
| 10° | 7.2 | 99.6% | 2.1 |
| 20° | 5.5 | 87.9% | 3.2 |
| 30° | 4.0 | 34.4% | 7.0 |
| 40° | 2.7 | 1.8% | 11.2 |

A test checks that, as the walls rise, the mean falls, availability never rises, and PDOP rises.

## How it's checked

- A cone gives exactly the same visibility and DOP as a mask of the same angle, at several places and times.
- A satellite counts as "blocked" exactly when it is above the horizon and below the walls. Switched-off satellites are never counted as blocked.
- In the browser there is one red line per blocked satellite. Switching the valley off restores the open sky.

## README

A6 is updated, A18 (the terrain model) is new, and the change log has an entry with the table above.

"""Colour pickers and random colours in the real page."""
import sys, time, colorsys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from cdp import Browser
results = []
def check(name, ok, detail=""):
    results.append(bool(ok)); print(("PASS " if ok else "FAIL ") + name + (f"  [{detail}]" if detail else ""))
def hsl(hexc):
    r, g, b = (int(hexc[i:i + 2], 16) / 255 for i in (1, 3, 5)); h, l, s = colorsys.rgb_to_hls(r, g, b); return h * 360, s, l
def gap(a, b): return min(abs(a - b), 360 - abs(a - b))
with Browser() as b:
    js = b.eval
    for _ in range(50):
        try: b.open("http://127.0.0.1:8766/"); break
        except Exception: time.sleep(0.2)
    b.wait("document.getElementById('status').textContent === 'Ready.'", 150)
    b.wait("document.getElementById('n').textContent !== '–'", 30)
    js("document.getElementById('tab-btn-cs').click()"); b.pump(0.3)
    colors = lambda: js("app.cons.decorate({}).colors")
    check("GPS starts blue on the globe and in the data", js("app.globe.satColor(0)") == "#3987e5" and colors()[0] == "#3987e5")
    # group colour picker
    js("const p = document.querySelector('#cs-list input[data-act=\"grp-color\"]'); p.value = '#22cc88'; p.dispatchEvent(new Event('input', {bubbles: true}))"); b.pump(0.3)
    check("dragging the group picker recolours the globe live", js("app.globe.satColor(5)") == "#22cc88")
    js("const p = document.querySelector('#cs-list input[data-act=\"grp-color\"]'); p.dispatchEvent(new Event('change', {bubbles: true}))"); b.pump(0.3)
    check("all 24 GPS satellites take the group colour", set(colors()) == {"#22cc88"})
    check("preset row swatch follows the group colour", "34, 204, 136" in js("document.querySelector('#cs-presets .swatch').style.background"))
    # one satellite
    js("const p = document.querySelector('#cs-list input[data-act=\"sat-color\"][data-i=\"3\"]'); p.value = '#ff00ff'; p.dispatchEvent(new Event('change', {bubbles: true}))"); b.pump(0.3)
    c = colors()
    check("a satellite picker changes only that satellite", c[3] == "#ff00ff" and c.count("#22cc88") == 23 and js("app.globe.satColor(3)") == "#ff00ff")
    js("const p = document.querySelector('#cs-list input[data-act=\"grp-color\"]'); p.value = '#3987e5'; p.dispatchEvent(new Event('change', {bubbles: true}))"); b.pump(0.3)
    check("setting the group colour again clears the satellite's own colour", set(colors()) == {"#3987e5"})
    # two Walker sets: one colour each, random, distinct, bright
    js("document.getElementById('cs-w-add').click()"); b.pump(0.3); js("document.getElementById('cs-w-add').click()"); b.pump(0.3)
    c = colors(); w1, w2 = set(c[24:36]), set(c[36:48])
    check("each new Walker set is one colour", len(w1) == 1 and len(w2) == 1, (w1, w2))
    h1, s1, l1 = hsl(w1.pop()); h2, s2, l2 = hsl(w2.pop()); hg = hsl("#3987e5")[0]
    check("their hues are far apart and far from GPS blue", gap(h1, h2) >= 40 and gap(h1, hg) >= 40 and gap(h2, hg) >= 40, f"{h1:.0f}, {h2:.0f} vs GPS {hg:.0f}")
    check("bright: saturation 0.7, lightness 0.6", abs(s1 - 0.7) < 0.02 and abs(l1 - 0.6) < 0.02 and abs(s2 - 0.7) < 0.02, f"s={s1:.2f}, l={l1:.2f}")
    # single satellites: each its own colour
    for _ in range(3): js("document.getElementById('cs-add').click()"); b.pump(0.2)
    singles = colors()[48:51]
    check("each added single satellite gets its own colour", len(set(singles)) == 3, singles)
    # randomness across page loads
    first = colors()[24]
    b.open("http://127.0.0.1:8766/"); b.wait("document.getElementById('status').textContent === 'Ready.'", 150); b.pump(0.5)
    js("document.getElementById('cs-w-add').click()"); b.pump(0.3)
    check("colours are random (a fresh page usually picks a different hue)", colors()[24] != first, f"{first} vs {colors()[24]}")
    b.screenshot("c_list.png")
    errs = [e for e in b.errors if "favicon" not in e]
    check("no JavaScript errors", not errs, errs[:4])
print(f"\n{sum(results)}/{len(results)} checks passed")
EOF

content.text:
The colours render correctly. The orange Walker satellites happen to sit on GPS orbits because the Walker form's defaults (20,200 km, 55°) overlap GPS. That's a default-value coincidence, not a bug. The four tabs now fit on one line.

Step 2, colours, is done. Nothing from this round is committed yet.

- **Colour pickers:** each constellation in the satellite list has a round colour swatch, and each satellite has its own.
  - The group swatch recolours the whole constellation and clears any per-satellite colours.
  - A satellite's swatch overrides only that satellite.
  - The globe updates live while you drag inside the picker.
- **Random colours:**
  - A new Walker set gets **one random colour for the whole set**, and each new single satellite gets its own.
  - The hue is chosen at random among the hues farthest from those already in use. Saturation is fixed at 70% and lightness at 60%, so it stays bright on the dark background.
  - Presets keep their fixed colours unless you change them.
- **Tested in the browser:** 12 of 12 checks pass. That includes globe colours matching the data, two Walker sets landing 111° apart in hue and far from GPS blue, and a fresh page picking a different colour. My first run failed on a bug in my test script (a repeated variable name), not the app.

The add forms still can't choose a colour themselves, so new additions are always random for now. That option comes with the Add dialog in step 4.

Shall I go on to step 3, the low-poly satellite models?

    inc, raan = np.radians(elements[:, INC]), np.radians(elements[:, RAAN])

def perigee_radius(elements):''')

    """The normal must be a unit vector perpendicular to the position at all times, and point along the
    angular momentum r x v (velocity from finite differences, independent of the formula)."""
    el = np.vstack([presets.gps(), presets.galileo(), presets.beidou_igso_geo(), ORBIT])
    n = c.orbit_normal(el)

        h = np.cross(r, finite_difference_velocity(el, t))
        assert np.allclose(h / np.linalg.norm(h, axis=1, keepdims=True), n, atol=1e-6)

Steps 3 and 4 are done and tested in headless Chrome, which finishes this round: Stage 4 plus the five interface features. All 182 Python tests and all seven browser suites pass. Steps 3 and 4 aren't committed yet.

## Step 4: the "Add satellites" pop-up and orbit preview

- **Constellation tab:** now just the satellite list, an **Add satellites…** button and Reset.
- **The dialog:** a floating panel over the globe, so the globe stays visible. It has **7 cards**, each with a picture of its satellite model that turns when you hover it:
  - GPS, Galileo, BeiDou MEO and BeiDou IGSO+GEO, which add or remove in one click. Added ones are marked ✓.
  - Single satellite, Geostationary and Walker constellation, which open their form inside the dialog with a Back button.
- **Colour:** each form has a colour choice, random by default. Picking a colour switches random off.
- **Orbit preview:** dashed rings and see-through satellite models on the globe for what you're about to add.
  - It appears when you hover a preset card, and updates live as you change values in a form or hover the Add button.
  - It disappears for an invalid orbit, and on Back or close.
- **Locking:** a Monte Carlo run closes the dialog and disables "Add satellites…" until it ends.
- **Python:** a new `api.preview()` returns the rings, positions and normals without adding anything. A test checks the positions match the orbits and that nothing gets added.
- **Walker default:** the form now defaults to a 12-satellite polar set at 1,200 km, so it no longer sits exactly on the GPS orbits.

## Testing

- **Dialog suite:** 23 of 23 browser checks pass.
  - All 7 card pictures are drawn.
  - The Galileo hover previews 3 rings and 24 satellites, and the Walker form previews 3 rings and 12 satellites.
  - A chosen colour reaches the globe.
- **Earlier suites:** every one still passes (Constellation 36, colours 12, step 5 30, Terrain 13, time 25, earlier features 14), with no JavaScript errors.
- **My scripts needed updating:** presets now live in the dialog's cards, so I updated those scripts. One edit lost its escaped quotes and caused a syntax error in my test, which I then fixed.

## README and port

- **README:** it lists `satmodels.js` and `thumbs.js`, and notes the models are drawn far larger than life and that their orientation doesn't affect any result.
- **Port:** I changed the README to **port 3000** to match your edit to `launch.sh`. Your `launch.sh` change shows as modified and will go into the next commit. `tools/serve.py` still defaults to 8000 if you run it without a port. Should I change that default to 3000 as well?

content.content:
2.0 Coverage Performance


   Coverage: The percentage of time over a specified time interval that a sufficient number of satellites
   are above a specified mask angle and provide an acceptable position solution geometry at any point
   on or near the Earth.


  Dilution of Precision (DOP): A Root Mean Square (RMS) measure of the effects that any given
  position solution geometry has on position errors. Geometry effects may be assessed in the local
  horizontal (HDOP), local vertical (VDOP), three-dimensional position (PDOP), or time (TDOP) for
  example.



          Coverage Standard                                      Conditions and Constraints
≥ 99.9% global average                       • Probability of 4 or more satellites in view over any 24 hour
                                               interval, averaged over the globe
                                             • 4 satellites must provide PDOP of 6 or less
                                             • 5° mask angle with no obscura
                                             • Standard is predicated on 24 operational satellites, as the
                                               constellation is defined in the almanac
≥ 96.9% at worst-case point                  • Probability of 4 or more satellites in view over any 24 hour
                                               interval, for the worst-case point on the globe
                                             • 4 satellites must provide PDOP of 6 or less
                                             • 5° mask angle with no obscura
                                             • Standard is predicated on 24 operational satellites, as the
                                               constellation is defined in the almanac


Almanacs for GPS weeks 1003 - 1016 used for this coverage portion of the report were obtained from the
Coast Guard web site (www.navcen.uscg.mil). Using these almanacs, an SPS coverage area program
developed by ACT-360 was used to calculate the PDOP at every 5o point between longitudes of 180W to
180E and 80S and 80N at one-minute intervals. This gives a total of 1440 samples for each of the 2376 grid
points in the coverage area. Table 2-1 provides the global averages and worst-case availability over a 24-
hour period for each week. Eight out of the fourteen days had Availabilities of 100%. The six days that
gave less than 100% availability were in Weeks 1006, 1007, 1013, 1014, 1015 and 1016. Table 2-1 also gives
the global 99.9% PDOP value for each of the 14 GPS Weeks. The PDOP was 5.02 or better 99.9% for each of
the 24-hour intervals.

The SPS program also produces a contour plot of the coverage area. Since the contour plots for each of the
fourteen days are similar, the day with the worst worst-case point and the highest 99.9% PDOP was selected
as the contour plot shown in this report. Figures 2-1 and 2-2 are the contour plot and satellite visibility plot
for GPS Week 1007. The contour plot shows that the highest PDOP was between 4 and 5 99.9% of the time.
Figure 2-2 shows that there were never less than 5 satellites visible at any time during the 24-hour interval.
At least 8 or more satellites were visible 88.4% of the time.

   Coverage: The percentage of time over a specified time interval that a sufficient number of satellites

  Dilution of Precision (DOP): A Root Mean Square (RMS) measure of the effects that any given

≥ 99.9% global average                       • Probability of 4 or more satellites in view over any 24 hour

Almanacs for GPS weeks 1003 - 1016 used for this coverage portion of the report were obtained from the
Coast Guard web site (www.navcen.uscg.mil). Using these almanacs, an SPS coverage area program
developed by ACT-360 was used to calculate the PDOP at every 5o point between longitudes of 180W to
180E and 80S and 80N at one-minute intervals. This gives a total of 1440 samples for each of the 2376 grid
points in the coverage area. Table 2-1 provides the global averages and worst-case availability over a 24-
hour period for each week. Eight out of the fourteen days had Availabilities of 100%. The six days that
gave less than 100% availability were in Weeks 1006, 1007, 1013, 1014, 1015 and 1016. Table 2-1 also gives
the global 99.9% PDOP value for each of the 14 GPS Weeks. The PDOP was 5.02 or better 99.9% for each of
the 24-hour intervals.
The SPS program also produces a contour plot of the coverage area. Since the contour plots for each of the
fourteen days are similar, the day with the worst worst-case point and the highest 99.9% PDOP was selected
as the contour plot shown in this report. Figures 2-1 and 2-2 are the contour plot and satellite visibility plot
for GPS Week 1007. The contour plot shows that the highest PDOP was between 4 and 5 99.9% of the time.
Figure 2-2 shows that there were never less than 5 satellites visible at any time during the 24-hour interval.
At least 8 or more satellites were visible 88.4% of the time.

Tables 3-6 and 3-7 show the statistics related to maximum PDOP and PDOP greater than six, respectively.
NOTE: Global in this report refers to the eight sites used. Although future reports will have all NSTB sites,
a true global availability cannot be determined since there aren’t reference stations around the world.
The increase in PDOP to above six in Honolulu was caused by a satellite outage. ACT-360 has developed
software to detect satellite outages. In Week 990 Day 1, the satellite monitoring software detected a 5-6
second outage on satellite PRN 18. This means that none of the receivers in the NSTB network tracked
Satellite 18 during these seconds. Although the receiver was still tracking 5 other satellites (PRN 7, 14, 15,
16 and 19), the geometry of the remaining satellites caused the PDOP to go above six.
The increase in PDOP to above six in Sitka was also caused by a satellite outage and was detected by the
satellite monitoring software. Satellite 17 was unavailable for about six seconds. This means that none of
the receivers in the NSTB network tracked Satellite 18 during these seconds. In this case, the Millenium
receiver was tracking eight other satellites (PRN 3, 6, 10, 13, 19, 22, 23 and 26).
The increases in Week 996 Day 5 and Week 1003 Day 3 in Winnipeg were due to a 5-6 second outage of
Satellite 18 that were also detected by the satellite monitoring software. The receiver was tracking five other
satellites in both cases. The other two increases were due to forecasted maintenance actions on Satellite 18
(NANU 1999024 and NANU 1999033). Solar storms were occurring in Week 999 Day 1. These storms may
have also contributed to the increases in PDOP by causing other satellites to be dropped or not tracked.
The data from the co-located GSV receiver in Winnipeg was processed for Week 1002 Day 3. The GSV

The search didn't turn up a direct download of a 1999 Yuma almanac, but it did surface the pieces you'd need to find one.

- **Archive location:** CelesTrak keeps Yuma almanacs in year-based archive pages, and its 1990 page is one example. The page lists the weekly files by date with their GPS week numbers, such as Dec 02 (0569). A 1999 page should follow the same pattern at celestrak.org/GPS/almanac/Yuma/1999/, though I didn't confirm that page exists.
- **NAVCEN pattern:** A MathWorks example builds NAVCEN URLs from the year and day of year, using a base path under navcen.uscg.gov/sites/default/files/gps/almanac/ with a yuma subfolder and a .alm extension. That suggests daily files, but I couldn't confirm that the 1999 files are still hosted there.
- **Week 1007 meaning:** Week 1007 is the IGS report week for days 115-121, dates 1999 Apr 25 - May 01. That is an orbit-analysis week, not an almanac listing.
- **Rollover issue:** Yuma files store the week modulo 1024, and the NAVCEN week count is based on the rollover, which last occurred in 1999. Since week 1007 falls before the August 1999 rollover, the almanac's week field should read 1007 directly. The rollover count is 0 before August 22, 1999 and 1 after it.

Next steps: check celestrak.org/GPS/almanac/Yuma/1999/ directly for the April–May 1999 files, and if they're missing, try the NAVCEN archive for those dates.

# Stage 5 plan: comparison with published data (FAA PAN Report #26, Langley 1999)

## Context
Stages 1-4 and the interface work are committed and pushed (`a05fc4e`; 182 Python tests; 7 browser suites). Stage 5 compares the model's output with published data in `paper/`. The project description recommends reproducing a published result.

What the papers offer:
- **FAA GPS SPS Performance Analysis Report #26 (1999), Table 2-1.** For GPS weeks 1003-1016 (28 Mar - 27 Jun 1999) it gives the global 99.9% PDOP (3.22-5.02), the global average availability (PDOP <= 6 with 4+ satellites, 5 deg mask: 99.963-100%) and the worst-case grid point (98.264-100%). Method: the weekly almanac; every 5 deg from 180W-175E and 80S-80N (2,376 points); every minute for 24 h; 5 deg mask. Figure 2-2 (week 1007): at the worst point, never fewer than 5 satellites in view, and 8 or more in view 88.4% of the time.
- **The almanacs the FAA used**, weeks 1003-1016, are online at CelesTrak (`celestrak.org/GPS/almanac/Yuma/1999/`).
- **Langley (1999)** gives exact values:
  - GDOP 1.581 for the tetrahedron (already tested) and 1.732 for one satellite at the zenith plus three on the horizon.
  - One satellite at the zenith plus three at 15 deg: HDOP 1.195 and VDOP 1.558; without solving for the clock, VDOP 0.913.
  - The highest possible elevation at the poles is about 45 deg.
  - Fredericton with a 5 deg mask: GDOP averages about 2 and never exceeds 3.5.
- **`paper/beidou.pdf`** is the official BDS B2b ICD (CSNO 2020), section 3.1. It confirms our BeiDou parameters: MEO altitude 21,528 km at 55 deg, IGSO 35,786 km at 55 deg, GEO 35,786 km at 80 / 110.5 / 140 deg E. The `papers.txt` entry moves from "reported" to "verified".

## Decisions made with the user
| Topic | Decision |
|---|---|
| Scope | **Reproduce FAA Table 2-1 with the real 1999 almanacs**, with **our ideal Walker 24/6/1** side by side; plus Langley's exact values |
| Computation | **Precompute in Python** (results committed); a **"Recompute this week"** button reruns one week in the browser's worker |
| Display | **Fifth tab "Compare"** with a **table and chart**; a **toggle for a PDOP map on the globe**; a **"GPS 1999" preset** in the Constellation tab |

## Proposed defaults (to confirm at approval)
- **Which 24 hours:** the FAA does not say which day of each week it used. We use the 24 h starting at each almanac's reference time (toa).
- **Satellites:** only those marked healthy (health 0) in the almanac.
- **Statistics:**
  - Global 99.9% PDOP = the 99.9th percentile of all point-minutes.
  - Global availability = the fraction of point-minutes with 4+ satellites and PDOP <= 6, every grid point weighted equally, as the FAA grid does. The area-weighted value is shown as well.
  - Worst point = the lowest availability over the 24 h at any grid point.
- **Orbits:** the standard GPS almanac algorithm (IS-GPS-200 Table 20-IV) for the real almanacs, with Earth-fixed positions and drifting orbit planes, using GPS's mu = 3.986005e14 and Earth rate 7.2921151467e-5.
  - The receiver stays on our sphere. The FAA presumably used the WGS-84 ellipsoid; the difference is a few km in receiver position and is negligible for DOP.
- **The "GPS 1999" preset:** week 1007, the week the FAA plotted, with the healthy satellites converted to our orbital elements so they sit in their true places on 1999-04-25 when the date picker is set there.
  - The slow drift of the orbit planes (about -0.04 deg/day) is ignored in the live view, so positions are right near that date and drift away over months.
  - The card says so.
- **PDOP map:** each 5 deg cell coloured by the 99.99th-percentile PDOP over the 24 h, the statistic of the FAA's contour map. It uses a one-hue sequential scale with a legend, the week and model can be chosen, and the cells turn with the Earth.

## Work
1. **Data**
   - Download the 14 YUMA almanacs to `web/data/almanac/1999/` (raw text, committed).
   - Transcribe Table 2-1, the Figure 2-2 statements and Langley's values into `web/data/published.json`, each with its page reference.
   - Update `papers.txt` (sources, retrieval date; BeiDou verified).
2. **Python**
   - `web/sim/almanac.py`: parse YUMA and compute Earth-fixed positions.
   - `web/sim/faa.py`: the FAA grid statistics for any satellite source, vectorized per minute block.
   - `dop()` gets an option to leave out the clock (needed for Langley's 0.913).
   - API entry points for the page and the worker.
   - Add the new modules to `pyloader.js` (the guard test enforces this).
3. **`tools/reproduce_faa.py`**: computes all 14 weeks for the real almanacs plus the ideal model and writes `web/data/faa_reproduction.json` (the table numbers and the per-point maps).
4. **Compare tab**
   - A table of published / real-almanac / ideal values per week, with the differences shown.
   - A chart of 99.9% PDOP per week (three series, legend, hover values).
   - Langley's exact values computed live, with pass/fail.
   - The PDOP-map toggle with week and model selectors.
   - "Recompute this week" in the worker, with a progress bar and a comparison of the result with the stored one.
5. **"GPS 1999" preset** (card in the Add dialog).
6. **README:** new assumptions (A19 almanac model, A20 FAA method choices), a change-log entry, the reproduction results and a discussion of any differences.

## Verification
- **Almanac parsing:**
  - Satellite counts and health flags are read correctly.
  - Values are in sensible ranges: sqrt(A) about 5153.6, e < 0.03, i about 55 deg.
  - One file is checked by hand against its text.
- **Almanac orbits:**
  - Radius = A(1 - e cos E).
  - Latitude never exceeds the inclination.
  - The ascending-node crossing happens at the longitude the almanac formula predicts (found numerically).
  - The period is about 11 h 58 min.
  - The sub-satellite track repeats after a sidereal day.
- **FAA method on the ideal model:** the mean in view agrees with the area-weighted analytic value in the limit (grid mean vs cap formula, within grid error), and availability is 100% for 24 satellites.
- **Langley:** GDOP 1.732; HDOP 1.195 and VDOP 1.558; VDOP 0.913 without the clock; pole maximum elevation 45.3 deg vs "about 45".
- **The reproduction itself (the science result):** our real-almanac 99.9% PDOP and availabilities against Table 2-1, week by week. Agreement or explained differences are reported honestly, not forced into a test.
- **Browser:**
  - The Compare tab table and chart render with values from the JSON.
  - The PDOP map toggles on and off and turns with the Earth.
  - Recompute matches the stored week.
  - The GPS 1999 preset loads its satellites and, on 1999-04-25, puts them near their almanac positions (checked against `almanac.py`).
  - No JavaScript errors.
  - All earlier suites still pass.

# Plan: Stage 4 (terrain) + colours, orbit preview, low-poly satellite models, "Add" selection screen

## Context
Stages 1-3 and the time controls are committed (`ece5497`; 171 Python tests; headless-Chrome suites pass). The user now asks for Stage 4 (blocking by obstacles) and five interface features: changeable colours, random colours for new groups and satellites, an orbit preview while adding, recognisable low-poly satellite models, and a selection screen for adding satellites.

## Decisions made with the user
| Topic | Decision |
|---|---|
| Terrain model | **Conical**: one blocking angle in every direction (the shape is a parameter, so other shapes can come later) |
| Monte Carlo | Same cone at every trial (orientation does not matter for a cone) |
| Visual | **Blocked sight lines drawn in another colour** (red, dashed) on the globe |
| Controls | **Fourth tab "Terrain"** |
| Colours | **Colour picker per group and per satellite** (a satellite's own colour overrides its group's). New groups get **one random bright hue**, chosen away from the existing groups' hues; each new single satellite gets its own random hue; presets keep their fixed colours. A colour chosen in the add form overrides the random one |
| Add screen | **Pop-up with cards, then the form**: GPS, Galileo, BeiDou MEO, BeiDou IGSO+GEO, Single satellite, Geostationary, Walker. Preset cards add directly; custom cards open their form in the dialog. The globe stays visible for the preview |
| Models | **Recognisable low-poly per system, ~20-60 triangles**: GPS III, Galileo, BeiDou-3, generic for added satellites. Body points at the Earth, wings along the orbit normal, drawn much larger than life, coloured by constellation (wings a darker shade) |

## Stage 4: terrain (conical valley)
- **Physics:** a satellite is usable if it is switched on and its elevation is at least the terrain's blocking angle in its direction. For a cone this is a constant, the same as the existing elevation mask. So **A13's analytic check applies unchanged** (already tested at masks of 0, 10 and 30 deg).
- **Python (`api.py`, `geometry.py`):** a terrain description `{"type": "cone", "angle_deg": e}` with `blocking_angle(az, terrain)` (constant for a cone; the hook for other shapes). `set_terrain(json)` stores it; `snapshot` uses it and also returns `blocked` (switched on, above the horizon, but below the terrain). The Monte Carlo receives the terrain angle (`mc_start` mask, already plumbed).
- **Terrain tab:** "Valley / obstacles" on/off, blocking angle (slider + number, 0-80 deg, default 20 when switched on), a short explanation and a small side-view diagram of the cone. It applies to the Live view and the Monte Carlo; the results header already shows the mask.
- **Globe:** sight lines to blocked satellites drawn red and dashed; visible ones stay green.
- **README:** A6 changed (the mask is now the terrain's blocking angle, set in the Terrain tab, default off = 0 deg); A18 (terrain model: conical, the same in all directions, no diffraction or partial blocking).

## Colours
- `constellation.js`: `colorOf(s) = s.color || group.color`. Swatches in the list are `<input type="color">` for each group header (sets the group and clears its satellites' own colours) and each satellite.
- Random hue: HSL with S 70%, L 60%; choose among 36 candidate hues the one farthest from the hues already used.
- Add forms: "Colour: random / pick" control.

## Orbit preview
- Python `preview(elements_json, t)` returns ring paths, current positions and orbit normals.
- `globe.setPreview(...)` / `clearPreview()`: bright dashed rings and semi-transparent ghost models.
- Shown while a custom form is valid and being edited, and while hovering a preset card or an Add button; cleared when the dialog closes or the form is invalid.

## Low-poly satellite models
- New `web/satmodels.js`: four merged `BufferGeometry` models built from boxes, plates and a low cone (dish), with vertex shading so the wings are a darker shade of the material colour. One material per satellite (colour), and one shared geometry per model.
- Python `set_constellation` also returns each satellite's orbit normal (unit vector), used to orient the wings: `mesh.up = normal; mesh.lookAt(Earth centre)`.
- Ghost (switched off), hover enlargement, picking and colours work as before (picking stays screen-space on positions).

## "Add satellites" selection screen
- The Constellation tab keeps the satellite list plus an **"Add satellites…"** button. The current add-satellite and Walker forms move into a floating dialog over the globe (non-modal, so the globe stays visible).
- Cards show a static thumbnail of the model, rendered once by one shared offscreen renderer; the hovered card's model turns.
- Card types: 4 presets (added directly; already present shows "Remove"), Single satellite (circular/elliptical), Geostationary (longitude), Walker T/P/F. Each form has the colour control and the live preview.

## Build order (report after each)
1. Terrain: Python + tests, Terrain tab, red blocked lines, README.
2. Colours (pickers, random hues).
3. Satellite models (+ normals).
4. Selection dialog + orbit preview.
5. Full browser regression and README.

## Verification
- **Python tests:**
  - A cone of angle e gives the same visibility and DOP as a mask of e.
  - `blocked` = above the horizon and below the cone, and switched-off satellites are never "blocked".
  - The Monte Carlo with a cone of 20 deg matches the analytic mean.
  - Availability falls monotonically as the cone angle rises.
  - Preview output: paths, positions on their rings, normals.
  - Normals are unit vectors, perpendicular to the position, and equal to r x v.
- **Browser (headless Chrome):**
  - The Terrain tab changes the count in view.
  - Red line count = blocked count.
  - Monte Carlo results use the angle.
  - The colour pickers change the globe and list colours.
  - New groups get one shared random colour, distinct from the others.
  - The dialog flows: preset adds, custom forms, cancel.
  - The preview appears on edit and hover and clears on close.
  - Models render (screenshots inspected).

# Stage 5 plan: comparison with published data (FAA PAN Report #26, Langley 1999)

## Context
Stages 1-4 and the interface work are committed and pushed (`a05fc4e`; 182 Python tests; 7 browser suites). Stage 5 compares the model's output with published data in `paper/`. The project description recommends reproducing a published result.

What the papers offer:
- **FAA GPS SPS Performance Analysis Report #26 (1999), Table 2-1.** For GPS weeks 1003-1016 (28 Mar - 27 Jun 1999) it gives the global 99.9% PDOP (3.22-5.02), the global average availability (PDOP <= 6 with 4+ satellites, 5 deg mask: 99.963-100%) and the worst-case grid point (98.264-100%). Method: the weekly almanac; every 5 deg from 180W-175E and 80S-80N (2,376 points); every minute for 24 h; 5 deg mask. Figure 2-2 (week 1007): at the worst point, never fewer than 5 satellites in view, and 8 or more in view 88.4% of the time.
- **The almanacs the FAA used**, weeks 1003-1016, are online at CelesTrak (`celestrak.org/GPS/almanac/Yuma/1999/`).
- **Langley (1999)** gives exact values:
  - GDOP 1.581 for the tetrahedron (already tested) and 1.732 for one satellite at the zenith plus three on the horizon.
  - One satellite at the zenith plus three at 15 deg: HDOP 1.195 and VDOP 1.558; without solving for the clock, VDOP 0.913.
  - The highest possible elevation at the poles is about 45 deg.
  - Fredericton with a 5 deg mask: GDOP averages about 2 and never exceeds 3.5.
- **`paper/beidou.pdf`** is the official BDS B2b ICD (CSNO 2020), section 3.1. It confirms our BeiDou parameters: MEO altitude 21,528 km at 55 deg, IGSO 35,786 km at 55 deg, GEO 35,786 km at 80 / 110.5 / 140 deg E. The `papers.txt` entry moves from "reported" to "verified".

## Decisions made with the user
| Topic | Decision |
|---|---|
| Scope | **Reproduce FAA Table 2-1 with the real 1999 almanacs**, with **our ideal Walker 24/6/1** side by side; plus Langley's exact values |
| Computation | **Precompute in Python** (results committed); a **"Recompute this week"** button reruns one week in the browser's worker |
| Display | **Fifth tab "Compare"** with a **table and chart**; a **toggle for a PDOP map on the globe**; a **"GPS 1999" preset** in the Constellation tab |

## Proposed defaults (to confirm at approval)
- **Which 24 hours:** the FAA does not say which day of each week it used. We use the 24 h starting at each almanac's reference time (toa).
- **Satellites:** only those marked healthy (health 0) in the almanac.
- **Statistics:**
  - Global 99.9% PDOP = the 99.9th percentile of all point-minutes.
  - Global availability = the fraction of point-minutes with 4+ satellites and PDOP <= 6, every grid point weighted equally, as the FAA grid does. The area-weighted value is shown as well.
  - Worst point = the lowest availability over the 24 h at any grid point.
- **Orbits:** the standard GPS almanac algorithm (IS-GPS-200 Table 20-IV) for the real almanacs, with Earth-fixed positions and drifting orbit planes, using GPS's mu = 3.986005e14 and Earth rate 7.2921151467e-5.
  - The receiver stays on our sphere. The FAA presumably used the WGS-84 ellipsoid; the difference is a few km in receiver position and is negligible for DOP.
- **The "GPS 1999" preset:** week 1007, the week the FAA plotted, with the healthy satellites converted to our orbital elements so they sit in their true places on 1999-04-25 when the date picker is set there.
  - The slow drift of the orbit planes (about -0.04 deg/day) is ignored in the live view, so positions are right near that date and drift away over months.
  - The card says so.
- **PDOP map:** each 5 deg cell coloured by the 99.99th-percentile PDOP over the 24 h, the statistic of the FAA's contour map. It uses a one-hue sequential scale with a legend, the week and model can be chosen, and the cells turn with the Earth.

## Work
1. **Data**
   - Download the 14 YUMA almanacs to `web/data/almanac/1999/` (raw text, committed).
   - Transcribe Table 2-1, the Figure 2-2 statements and Langley's values into `web/data/published.json`, each with its page reference.
   - Update `papers.txt` (sources, retrieval date; BeiDou verified).
2. **Python**
   - `web/sim/almanac.py`: parse YUMA and compute Earth-fixed positions.
   - `web/sim/faa.py`: the FAA grid statistics for any satellite source, vectorized per minute block.
   - `dop()` gets an option to leave out the clock (needed for Langley's 0.913).
   - API entry points for the page and the worker.
   - Add the new modules to `pyloader.js` (the guard test enforces this).
3. **`tools/reproduce_faa.py`**: computes all 14 weeks for the real almanacs plus the ideal model and writes `web/data/faa_reproduction.json` (the table numbers and the per-point maps).
4. **Compare tab**
   - A table of published / real-almanac / ideal values per week, with the differences shown.
   - A chart of 99.9% PDOP per week (three series, legend, hover values).
   - Langley's exact values computed live, with pass/fail.
   - The PDOP-map toggle with week and model selectors.
   - "Recompute this week" in the worker, with a progress bar and a comparison of the result with the stored one.
5. **"GPS 1999" preset** (card in the Add dialog).
6. **README:** new assumptions (A19 almanac model, A20 FAA method choices), a change-log entry, the reproduction results and a discussion of any differences.

## Verification
- **Almanac parsing:**
  - Satellite counts and health flags are read correctly.
  - Values are in sensible ranges: sqrt(A) about 5153.6, e < 0.03, i about 55 deg.
  - One file is checked by hand against its text.
- **Almanac orbits:**
  - Radius = A(1 - e cos E).
  - Latitude never exceeds the inclination.
  - The ascending-node crossing happens at the longitude the almanac formula predicts (found numerically).
  - The period is about 11 h 58 min.
  - The sub-satellite track repeats after a sidereal day.
- **FAA method on the ideal model:** the mean in view agrees with the area-weighted analytic value in the limit (grid mean vs cap formula, within grid error), and availability is 100% for 24 satellites.
- **Langley:** GDOP 1.732; HDOP 1.195 and VDOP 1.558; VDOP 0.913 without the clock; pole maximum elevation 45.3 deg vs "about 45".
- **The reproduction itself (the science result):** our real-almanac 99.9% PDOP and availabilities against Table 2-1, week by week. Agreement or explained differences are reported honestly, not forced into a test.
- **Browser:**
  - The Compare tab table and chart render with values from the JSON.
  - The PDOP map toggles on and off and turns with the Earth.
  - Recompute matches the stored week.
  - The GPS 1999 preset loads its satellites and, on 1999-04-25, puts them near their almanac positions (checked against `almanac.py`).
  - No JavaScript errors.
  - All earlier suites still pass.

input.content:
"""Real GPS orbits from almanacs (YUMA text format), as broadcast by the satellites.

The almanac gives, for each satellite, Kepler elements at a reference time toa (seconds into
the GPS week) plus the slow drift of the orbit plane. Positions follow the standard user
algorithm of the GPS interface specification IS-GPS-200 (Table 20-IV), simplified as the
almanac allows (no harmonic corrections). The result is Earth-fixed (ECEF): x toward
longitude 0, z toward the north pole.

Used for Stage 5: reproducing the FAA's 1999 coverage statistics with the real constellation.
"""

import datetime as dt
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

from . import constellation, geometry

MU_GPS = 3.986005e14              # m^3/s^2, the value GPS uses (IS-GPS-200)
OMEGA_E_GPS = 7.2921151467e-5     # rad/s, Earth rotation rate GPS uses
GPS_EPOCH = dt.datetime(1980, 1, 6)          # start of GPS week 0 (GPS time)
GPS_MINUS_UTC_1999 = 13.0                    # seconds: leap seconds between GPS time and UTC in 1999

ALMANAC_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "almanac" / "1999"

# YUMA field names -> our keys
_FIELDS = {
    "ID": "prn", "Health": "health", "Eccentricity": "e", "Time of Applicability(s)": "toa",
    "Orbital Inclination(rad)": "i0", "Rate of Right Ascen(r/s)": "omega_dot", "SQRT(A)  (m^1/2)": "sqrt_a",
    "Right Ascen at TOA(rad)": "omega0", "Argument of Perigee(rad)": "argp", "Mean Anom(rad)": "m0", "week": "week",
}


def parse_yuma(text):
    """List of satellites, each a dict with prn, health, e, toa, i0, omega_dot, sqrt_a, omega0,
    argp, m0 (radians and seconds as in the file) and week."""
    satellites, current = [], None
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if line.startswith("****"):
            current = {}
            satellites.append(current)
            continue
        if ":" not in line or current is None:
            continue
        name, value = line.split(":", 1)
        key = _FIELDS.get(name.strip()) or _FIELDS.get(name.rstrip())
        if key:
            current[key] = int(value) if key in ("prn", "health", "week") else float(value)
    return satellites


def load_week(week, healthy_only=True):
    """The almanac for one GPS week of 1999 (weeks 1003-1016 are in the repository)."""
    path = next(ALMANAC_DIR.glob(f"almanac.yuma.week{week}.*.txt"))
    sats = parse_yuma(path.read_text())
    return [s for s in sats if s["health"] == 0] if healthy_only else sats


def _arrays(sats):
    return {k: np.array([s[k] for s in sats], dtype=float) for k in ("e", "toa", "i0", "omega_dot", "sqrt_a", "omega0", "argp", "m0")}


def ecef_positions(sats, t):
    """Earth-fixed positions (km) of the satellites at GPS time t, given as seconds from the start
    of the almanac's week (t may exceed one week; it is not wrapped). t may be an array: the
    result then has shape (..., N, 3)."""
    a = _arrays(sats)

"""The FAA's coverage method (GPS SPS Performance Analysis Report #26, section 2), for any satellites.

Grid: every 5 deg from 180W to 175E (72 longitudes) and 80S to 80N (33 latitudes): 2,376 points.
Time: every minute for 24 h (1,440 samples). Mask: 5 deg. A sample is "good" if 4 or more satellites
are above the mask and PDOP <= 6. Reported per day:
  - global 99.9% PDOP: the 99.9th percentile of PDOP over all point-minutes (undefined PDOP, fewer than
    4 satellites, counts as infinitely bad);
  - global average: the percentage of good point-minutes, every grid point weighted equally (as on the
    FAA's grid); the area-weighted value (cos latitude) is given too;
  - worst-case point: the lowest percentage of good minutes at any one grid point;
and, for the maps, each point's 99.99th-percentile PDOP (the statistic of the FAA's contour plot).
Everything is computed in the Earth-fixed frame, where the grid points do not move.
"""

import numpy as np

from . import geometry
from .dop import dop_batch

GRID_LATS = np.arange(-80.0, 80.1, 5.0)          # 33
GRID_LONS = np.arange(-180.0, 180.0, 5.0)        # 72
MASK_DEG = 5.0
PDOP_MAX = 6.0
MINUTES = 1440


def grid():
    lat, lon = np.meshgrid(GRID_LATS, GRID_LONS, indexing="ij")
    return lat.ravel(), lon.ravel()               # 2,376 points, latitude-major


class Coverage:
    """Accumulates the FAA statistics minute by minute, so a long run can report progress.

    positions_at(t_array) must return Earth-fixed satellite positions (km), shape (len(t), N, 3), for
    the times t_array (any time unit the caller likes: these are just labels passed through)."""

    def __init__(self, positions_at, times, mask_deg=MASK_DEG, pdop_max=PDOP_MAX):
        self.positions_at, self.times = positions_at, np.asarray(times, dtype=float)
        self.mask_deg, self.pdop_max = mask_deg, pdop_max
        self.lat, self.lon = grid()
        self.rx = geometry.earth_fixed_position(self.lat, self.lon)      # (M, 3)
        self.enu = geometry.earth_fixed_enu(self.lat, self.lon)         # (M, 3, 3)
        M, T = len(self.lat), len(self.times)
        self.pdop = np.full((T, M), np.inf)          # inf where undefined (counts as bad)
        self.nvis = np.zeros((T, M), dtype=np.int16)
        self.done = 0

    def advance(self, n_minutes):
        """Compute the next n_minutes samples. Returns the fraction done."""
        stop = min(len(self.times), self.done + int(n_minutes))
        M = len(self.lat)
        for k in range(self.done, stop):
            sat = self.positions_at(self.times[k:k + 1])[0]                         # (N, 3)
            sats = np.broadcast_to(sat, (M,) + sat.shape)
            _, el, unit = geometry.look_angles(self.rx, sats, self.enu)
            visible = el >= self.mask_deg
            p = dop_batch(unit, visible, self.enu)["pdop"]
            self.pdop[k] = np.where(np.isnan(p), np.inf, p)
            self.nvis[k] = visible.sum(axis=1)
        self.done = stop
        return self.done / len(self.times)

    def results(self):
        d = self.done
        pdop, nvis = self.pdop[:d], self.nvis[:d]
        good = (nvis >= 4) & (pdop <= self.pdop_max)
        per_point = good.mean(axis=0)                                               # (M,)
        weights = np.cos(np.radians(self.lat))
        worst = int(np.argmin(per_point))
        return {
            "minutes": d,
            "global_999_pdop": float(np.percentile(pdop, 99.9)),
            "global_average_pct": 100.0 * float(good.mean()),
            "global_average_area_weighted_pct": 100.0 * float(np.average(per_point, weights=weights)),
            "worst_point_pct": 100.0 * float(per_point[worst]),
            "worst_point": {"lat": float(self.lat[worst]), "lon": float(self.lon[worst]),
                            "min_visible": int(nvis[:, worst].min()),
                            "pct_time_8_or_more_visible": 100.0 * float((nvis[:, worst] >= 8).mean())},
            "mean_visible": float(nvis.mean()),
            "mean_visible_area_weighted": float(np.average(nvis.mean(axis=0), weights=weights)),
            "max_pdop": float(pdop.max()),
            # map: each point's 99.99th-percentile PDOP (inf -> null in JSON is done by the caller)
            "point_9999_pdop": np.percentile(pdop, 99.99, axis=0).tolist(),
        }

import sys, json, numpy as np

from sim import almanac as al, faa

    s = al.load_week(week); toa = s[0]["toa"]

    per999 = np.percentile(P, 99.9, axis=0)
    per_max = P.max(axis=0)

        "mean over points of per-point 99.9th": per999[np.isfinite(per999)].mean(),

        "median over points of per-point 99.9th": np.median(per999),
        "mean over points of per-point max": per_max[np.isfinite(per_max)].mean(),
        "pooled 99.9th, area-weighted": None,
    }

    vals = P.ravel(); wts = np.tile(w, P.shape[0]); order = np.argsort(vals); cw = np.cumsum(wts[order]) / wts.sum()

EOF

"""The FAA's coverage method (GPS SPS Performance Analysis Report #26, section 2), for any satellites.

Grid: every 5 deg from 180W to 175E (72 longitudes) and 80S to 80N (33 latitudes): 2,376 points.
Time: every minute for 24 h (1,440 samples). Mask: 5 deg. A sample is "good" if 4 or more satellites
are above the mask and PDOP <= 6. Reported per day:
  - global 99.9% PDOP: the 99.9th percentile of PDOP over all point-minutes (undefined PDOP, fewer than
    4 satellites, counts as infinitely bad);
  - global average: the percentage of good point-minutes, every grid point weighted equally (as on the
    FAA's grid); the area-weighted value (cos latitude) is given too;
  - worst-case point: the lowest percentage of good minutes at any one grid point;
and, for the maps, each point's 99.99th-percentile PDOP (the statistic of the FAA's contour plot).
Everything is computed in the Earth-fixed frame, where the grid points do not move.
"""

import numpy as np

from . import geometry
from .dop import dop_batch

GRID_LATS = np.arange(-80.0, 80.1, 5.0)          # 33
GRID_LONS = np.arange(-180.0, 180.0, 5.0)        # 72
MASK_DEG = 5.0
PDOP_MAX = 6.0
MINUTES = 1440


def grid():
    lat, lon = np.meshgrid(GRID_LATS, GRID_LONS, indexing="ij")
    return lat.ravel(), lon.ravel()               # 2,376 points, latitude-major


class Coverage:
    """Accumulates the FAA statistics minute by minute, so a long run can report progress.

    positions_at(t_array) must return Earth-fixed satellite positions (km), shape (len(t), N, 3), for
    the times t_array (any time unit the caller likes: these are just labels passed through)."""

    def __init__(self, positions_at, times, mask_deg=MASK_DEG, pdop_max=PDOP_MAX):
        self.positions_at, self.times = positions_at, np.asarray(times, dtype=float)
        self.mask_deg, self.pdop_max = mask_deg, pdop_max
        self.lat, self.lon = grid()
        self.rx = geometry.earth_fixed_position(self.lat, self.lon)      # (M, 3)
        self.enu = geometry.earth_fixed_enu(self.lat, self.lon)         # (M, 3, 3)
        M, T = len(self.lat), len(self.times)
        self.pdop = np.full((T, M), np.inf)          # inf where undefined (counts as bad)
        self.nvis = np.zeros((T, M), dtype=np.int16)
        self.done = 0

    def advance(self, n_minutes):
        """Compute the next n_minutes samples. Returns the fraction done."""
        stop = min(len(self.times), self.done + int(n_minutes))
        M = len(self.lat)
        for k in range(self.done, stop):
            sat = self.positions_at(self.times[k:k + 1])[0]                         # (N, 3)
            sats = np.broadcast_to(sat, (M,) + sat.shape)
            _, el, unit = geometry.look_angles(self.rx, sats, self.enu)
            visible = el >= self.mask_deg
            p = dop_batch(unit, visible, self.enu)["pdop"]
            self.pdop[k] = np.where(np.isnan(p), np.inf, p)
            self.nvis[k] = visible.sum(axis=1)
        self.done = stop
        return self.done / len(self.times)

    def results(self):
        d = self.done
        pdop, nvis = self.pdop[:d], self.nvis[:d]
        good = (nvis >= 4) & (pdop <= self.pdop_max)
        per_point = good.mean(axis=0)                                               # (M,)
        weights = np.cos(np.radians(self.lat))
        worst = int(np.argmin(per_point))
        return {
            "minutes": d,
            "global_999_pdop": float(np.percentile(pdop, 99.9)),
            "global_average_pct": 100.0 * float(good.mean()),
            "global_average_area_weighted_pct": 100.0 * float(np.average(per_point, weights=weights)),
            "worst_point_pct": 100.0 * float(per_point[worst]),
            "worst_point": {"lat": float(self.lat[worst]), "lon": float(self.lon[worst]),
                            "min_visible": int(nvis[:, worst].min()),
                            "pct_time_8_or_more_visible": 100.0 * float((nvis[:, worst] >= 8).mean())},
            "mean_visible": float(nvis.mean()),
            "mean_visible_area_weighted": float(np.average(nvis.mean(axis=0), weights=weights)),
            "max_pdop": float(pdop.max()),
            # map: each point's 99.99th-percentile PDOP (inf -> null in JSON is done by the caller)
            "point_9999_pdop": np.percentile(pdop, 99.99, axis=0).tolist(),
        }

Writes web/data/faa_reproduction.json (the numbers the Compare tab shows, and the PDOP maps).
Takes about 7 minutes. Run from the project root:   python tools/reproduce_faa.py
"""

import json
import math
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "web"))
from sim import almanac, constellation, faa, geometry, presets  # noqa: E402

OUTPUT = ROOT / "web" / "data" / "faa_reproduction.json"
PUBLISHED = json.loads((ROOT / "web" / "data" / "published.json").read_text())["faa_pan26"]["table_2_1"]["rows"]
WEEKS = range(1003, 1017)

# Satellite sets that were tried because the healthy-only result did not match the published row.
EXPLANATIONS = {
    1012: {"label": "keep PRN 15 (flagged unhealthy in this almanac)", "exclude": []},
    1014: {"label": "drop only PRN 15 (keep PRN 16)", "exclude": [15]},
    1016: {"label": "drop only PRN 15 (keep PRN 9)", "exclude": [15]},
    1007: {"label": "no single missing satellite found that reproduces this row (best tried: without PRN 15)", "exclude": [15]},
}


def clean(x):
    """inf/NaN are not valid JSON."""
    if isinstance(x, float) and not math.isfinite(x):
        return None
    if isinstance(x, list):
        return [clean(v) for v in x]
    if isinstance(x, dict):
        return {k: clean(v) for k, v in x.items()}
    return x


def run_almanac(sats):
    toa = sats[0]["toa"]
    cov = faa.Coverage(lambda tt: almanac.ecef_positions(sats, tt), toa + 60.0 * np.arange(faa.MINUTES))
    cov.advance(faa.MINUTES)
    return cov.results()


def round_map(values):
    return [None if not math.isfinite(v) else round(v, 2) for v in values]


def main():
    start = time.time()
    out = {"grid": {"lats": faa.GRID_LATS.tolist(), "lons": faa.GRID_LONS.tolist()},
           "method": "24 h from each almanac's reference time, every minute; 5 deg mask; good = 4+ satellites and PDOP <= 6",
           "weeks": []}

    el = presets.gps()                                  # the ideal model does not change from week to week
    cov = faa.Coverage(lambda tt: geometry.inertial_to_earth_fixed(constellation.positions(el, tt), tt), 60.0 * np.arange(faa.MINUTES))
    cov.advance(faa.MINUTES)
    ideal = cov.results()
    ideal_map = round_map(ideal.pop("point_9999_pdop"))
    out["ideal"] = clean({**ideal, "map_9999_pdop": ideal_map, "satellites": 24})
    print(f"ideal Walker 24/6/1: {ideal['global_999_pdop']:.2f}  {ideal['global_average_pct']:.3f}%  {ideal['worst_point_pct']:.3f}%", flush=True)

    for row in PUBLISHED:
        week = row[0]
        sats = almanac.load_week(week)
        all_sats = almanac.load_week(week, healthy_only=False)
        r = run_almanac(sats)
        week_map = round_map(r.pop("point_9999_pdop"))
        entry = {"week": week, "toa_utc": almanac.toa_datetime_utc(sats).isoformat(),
                 "published": dict(zip(["global_999_pdop", "global_average_pct", "worst_point_pct"], row[1:])),
                 "real": {**r, "satellites": len(sats), "unhealthy_prns": [s["prn"] for s in all_sats if s["health"] != 0]},
                 "map_9999_pdop": week_map}
        if week in EXPLANATIONS:
            e = EXPLANATIONS[week]
            alt = run_almanac([s for s in all_sats if s["prn"] not in e["exclude"]])
            alt.pop("point_9999_pdop")
            entry["explanation"] = {**e, "result": alt}
        out["weeks"].append(clean(entry))
        print(f"{week}: published {row[1]:.2f} {row[2]:.3f} {row[3]:.3f} | ours {r['global_999_pdop']:.2f} "
              f"{r['global_average_pct']:.3f} {r['worst_point_pct']:.3f}  ({time.time() - start:.0f} s)", flush=True)

    OUTPUT.write_text(json.dumps(out, separators=(",", ":")))
    print(f"wrote {OUTPUT.relative_to(ROOT)} ({OUTPUT.stat().st_size // 1024} KB)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Stage 5: real 1999 GPS almanacs, the FAA coverage method, and Langley's worked DOP values."""

import datetime as dt
import json
import math
import re
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pytest

from sim import almanac as al
from sim import api, constellation as c, faa, geometry as g, presets
from sim.dop import dop

WEB = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "web"


# ---- almanac parsing -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_parse_week_1007_against_the_file_text():
    """PRN 1 of week 1007, read off the file by eye: e = 4.8365592957E-003, sqrt(A) = 5154.285156,
    inclination 0.9570926428 rad, Right Ascen at TOA -1.4810622931, toa 589824, week 1007."""
    sats = al.load_week(1007, healthy_only=False)
    assert len(sats) == 27
    p1 = sats[0]
    assert p1["prn"] == 1 and p1["health"] == 0 and p1["week"] == 1007 and p1["toa"] == 589824.0
    assert p1["e"] == 4.8365592957e-3 and p1["sqrt_a"] == 5154.285156
    assert p1["i0"] == 0.9570926428 and p1["omega0"] == -1.4810622931


@pytest.mark.parametrize("week", range(1003, 1017))
def test_every_almanac_is_sensible(week):
    sats = al.load_week(week, healthy_only=False)
    assert 24 <= len(sats) <= 32 and all(s["week"] == week for s in sats)
    for s in sats:
        assert abs(s["sqrt_a"] - 5153.6) < 5 and 0 <= s["e"] < 0.03 and abs(math.degrees(s["i0"]) - 55) < 5


def test_reference_time_is_in_its_week():
    t = al.toa_datetime_utc(al.load_week(1007))
    assert dt.datetime(1999, 4, 25) <= t < dt.datetime(1999, 5, 2)          # week 1007 = 25 Apr - 1 May 1999


# ---- almanac orbits ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SATS = al.load_week(1007)
TOA = SATS[0]["toa"]


def test_orbit_radius_and_latitude():
    t = TOA + np.linspace(0, 86400, 300)
    p = al.ecef_positions(SATS, t)                                       # (300, N, 3)
    r = np.linalg.norm(p, axis=2)
    for k, s in enumerate(SATS):
        A = s["sqrt_a"] ** 2 / 1000
        assert r[:, k].min() >= A * (1 - s["e"]) - 1e-6 and r[:, k].max() <= A * (1 + s["e"]) + 1e-6
    lat = np.degrees(np.arcsin(p[..., 2] / r))
    assert np.all(np.abs(lat) <= np.degrees([s["i0"] for s in SATS]) + 1e-9)


def test_period_is_about_11h58m():
    A = SATS[0]["sqrt_a"] ** 2
    assert abs(2 * math.pi * math.sqrt(A**3 / al.MU_GPS) / 3600 - 11.967) < 0.02


def test_ground_track_repeats_after_a_sidereal_day():
    """Two orbits per sidereal day: the point below each satellite comes back to (almost) the same place."""
    p0 = al.ecef_positions(SATS, TOA)
    p1 = al.ecef_positions(SATS, TOA + g.T_SIDEREAL)
    angle = np.degrees(np.arccos(np.sum(p0 * p1, axis=1) / np.linalg.norm(p0, axis=1) / np.linalg.norm(p1, axis=1)))
    assert angle.max() < 1.0


def test_ascending_node_is_where_the_almanac_formula_says():
    """Find numerically when satellite 0 crosses the equator going north; its longitude there must be
    Omega0 + (Omega_dot - OmegaE) tk - OmegaE toa (the node longitude of IS-GPS-200)."""
    s = SATS[0]
    t = TOA + np.arange(0, 43200, 1.0)
    z = al.ecef_positions(SATS[:1], t)[:, 0, 2]
    k = np.nonzero((z[:-1] < 0) & (z[1:] >= 0))[0][0]
    tc = t[k] + (0 - z[k]) / (z[k + 1] - z[k])                            # interpolate the crossing
    x, y, _ = al.ecef_positions(SATS[:1], tc)[0]
    node = s["omega0"] + (s["omega_dot"] - al.OMEGA_E_GPS) * (tc - s["toa"]) - al.OMEGA_E_GPS * s["toa"]
    assert abs((math.degrees(math.atan2(y, x) - node) + 180) % 360 - 180) < 1e-3


def test_gps_1999_preset_puts_satellites_where_the_almanac_does():
    """At the almanac's reference time (on our timeline) the preset's satellites are exactly at the
    almanac positions; a day later they are within 20 km (the plane drift is left out)."""
    el = presets.gps_1999()
    t_toa = (al.toa_datetime_utc(SATS) - dt.datetime(2026, 1, 1)).total_seconds()
    for hours, tol in ((0, 1e-6), (24, 20.0)):
        ours = g.inertial_to_earth_fixed(c.positions(el, t_toa + 3600 * hours), t_toa + 3600 * hours)
        assert np.abs(ours - al.ecef_positions(SATS, TOA + 3600 * hours)).max() < tol


# ---- the FAA coverage method --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_grid_is_the_faas():
    lat, lon = faa.grid()
    assert len(lat) == 2376 and lat.min() == -80 and lat.max() == 80 and lon.min() == -180 and lon.max() == 175


def test_ideal_model_by_the_faa_method():
    """A short run (2 hours) on the ideal 24 satellites: everything is good, and the grid's mean number
    in view is close to the analytic value (the grid stops at 80 deg and the samples are few)."""
    el = presets.gps()
    cov = faa.Coverage(lambda tt: g.inertial_to_earth_fixed(c.positions(el, tt), tt), 60.0 * np.arange(120))
    cov.advance(120)
    r = cov.results()
    assert r["global_average_pct"] == 100.0 and r["worst_point_pct"] == 100.0
    from sim import montecarlo as mc
    assert abs(r["mean_visible_area_weighted"] - mc.expected_mean_visible(el, 5.0)) < 0.15
    assert r["global_999_pdop"] < r["global_999_pdop_pooled"]          # the per-point mean is the smaller one


def test_reproduction_file_matches_the_published_table_in_the_clean_weeks():
    """The stored reproduction (tools/reproduce_faa.py) against Table 2-1 in the weeks whose satellite set
    is not in doubt: availabilities to 0.01 percentage points, the 99.9% PDOP within 0.06."""
    data = json.loads((WEB / "data" / "faa_reproduction.json").read_text())
    for w in data["weeks"]:
        if w["week"] in (1003, 1004, 1005, 1006, 1013, 1015):
            pub, ours = w["published"], w["real"]
            assert abs(ours["global_average_pct"] - pub["global_average_pct"]) < 0.01, w["week"]

"""Stage 5 in the real page: Compare tab, PDOP map, recompute, GPS 1999 preset."""
import sys, time, re
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from cdp import Browser
results = []
def check(name, ok, detail=""):
    results.append(bool(ok)); print(("PASS " if ok else "FAIL ") + name + (f"  [{detail}]" if detail else ""))
import urllib.request
for _ in range(50):
    try: urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:8766/"); break
    except OSError: time.sleep(0.2)
with Browser() as b:
    js = b.eval
    b.open("http://127.0.0.1:8766/")
    b.wait("document.getElementById('status').textContent === 'Ready.' || document.getElementById('status').textContent.startsWith('Error')", 180)
    check("page ready with the almanacs loaded", js("document.getElementById('status').textContent") == "Ready.", js("document.getElementById('status').textContent"))
    b.wait("document.getElementById('n').textContent !== '–'", 30)
    text = lambda id: js(f"document.getElementById('{id}').textContent")
    js("document.getElementById('tab-btn-cmp').click()"); b.pump(0.6)
    check("Compare tab shown", not js("document.getElementById('tab-cmp').hidden"))
    check("table has 14 weeks", js("document.querySelectorAll('#cmp-table tr[data-week]').length") == 14)
    print("   ", text("cmp-summary"))
    nonblank = js("(() => { const c = document.getElementById('cmp-chart'); const d = c.getContext('2d').getImageData(0, 0, c.width, c.height).data; let n = 0; for (let i = 3; i < d.length; i += 4) if (d[i]) n++; return n; })()")
    check("chart is drawn", nonblank > 1000, nonblank)
    b.screenshot("cmp_tab.png")
    js("document.getElementById('cmp-metric').value = 'worst_point_pct'; document.getElementById('cmp-metric').dispatchEvent(new Event('change'))"); b.pump(0.3)
    print("   ", text("cmp-summary"))
    check("metric switch updates the summary", "Worst-case point" in text("cmp-summary"))
    js("document.querySelector('#cmp-table tr[data-week=\"1014\"]').click()"); b.pump(0.3)
    check("week 1014 details include the satellite-set explanation", "drop only PRN 15" in text("cmp-details"), text("cmp-details")[-160:])
    js("document.getElementById('cmp-map').click()"); b.pump(0.6)
    check("PDOP map on the globe: 2,376 cells", js("app.globe.groundMapCells()") == 2376, js("app.globe.groundMapCells()"))
    b.screenshot("cmp_map.png")
    js("document.getElementById('cmp-map-source').value = 'ideal'; document.getElementById('cmp-map-source').dispatchEvent(new Event('change'))"); b.pump(0.4)
    check("switching the map to the ideal model", js("app.globe.groundMapCells()") == 2376 and "Ideal" in text("cmp-map-note"))
    js("document.getElementById('cmp-map').click()"); b.pump(0.3)
    check("map off", js("app.globe.groundMapCells()") == 0)
    rows = js("[...document.querySelectorAll('#cmp-langley tbody tr')].map(r => r.lastElementChild.textContent)")
    check("all Langley checks pass", len(rows) == 9 and all(r == "✓" for r in rows), rows)
    # recompute one week in the worker
    js("document.querySelector('#cmp-table tr[data-week=\"1003\"]').click()"); b.pump(0.2)
    js("document.getElementById('cmp-recompute').click()")
    b.wait("document.getElementById('cmp-recompute-msg').textContent.startsWith('Done') || document.getElementById('cmp-recompute-msg').textContent.startsWith('Error')", 400)
    msg = text("cmp-recompute-msg")
    check("recomputing week 1003 in the browser gives the stored result", "identical to the stored result" in msg, msg)
    # GPS 1999 preset
    js("document.getElementById('tab-btn-cs').click(); app.cons.openDialog()"); b.pump(0.4)
    js("document.querySelector('#cs-presets .card[data-key=\"gps_1999\"]').click()"); b.pump(0.6)
    check("GPS 1999 preset adds its 27 satellites", js("app.cons.count()") == 51, js("app.cons.count()"))
    js("app.cons.closeDialog(); document.getElementById('tab-btn-live').click()")
    js("document.getElementById('date').value = '1999-05-01'; document.getElementById('date').dispatchEvent(new Event('change'))")
    js("document.getElementById('time').value = String(19*60+50); document.getElementById('time').dispatchEvent(new Event('input'))"); b.pump(0.8)
    check("timeline at the almanac's date", text("tlabel").startswith("1999-05-01 19:50"), text("tlabel"))
    b.screenshot("cmp_1999.png")
    errs = [e for e in b.errors if "favicon" not in e]
    check("no JavaScript errors", not errs, errs[:4])
print(f"\n{sum(results)}/{len(results)} checks passed")
EOF
