import pathlib, json
p = pathlib.Path("README.md"); s = p.read_text()
def sub(old, new):
    global s
    assert s.count(old) == 1, (old[:60], s.count(old)); s = s.replace(old, new)

sub("| Local web server (no caching) | `tools/serve.py`, started by `launch.sh` |",
    "| Real GPS orbits from 1999 almanacs (IS-GPS-200 algorithm) | `web/sim/almanac.py`, almanacs in `web/data/almanac/1999/` |\n"
    "| The FAA's coverage method; the reproduction of its Table 2-1 | `web/sim/faa.py`, `tools/reproduce_faa.py` -> `web/data/faa_reproduction.json` |\n"
    "| Compare tab (table, chart, PDOP map, Langley's values) and the published numbers | `web/compare.js`, `web/data/published.json` |\n"
    "| Local web server (no caching) | `tools/serve.py`, started by `launch.sh` |")

lines = s.split("\n")
j = next(k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("| A18 |"))
lines[j + 1:j + 1] = [
    "| A19 | **Real 1999 GPS orbits** (Stage 5) come from the weekly almanacs, propagated with the standard almanac algorithm of IS-GPS-200 "
    "(Kepler orbit, drifting orbit plane, GPS's mu = 3.986005e14 m^3/s^2 and Earth rate 7.2921151467e-5 rad/s) | only the satellites flagged healthy; "
    "GPS time is taken as UTC + 13 s (1999). For the live 'GPS 1999' preset the plane drift (about -0.04 deg/day) is left out, so the satellites are "
    "exactly where the almanac puts them on 1999-05-01 19:50 UTC and drift from it by about 18 km per day | `almanac.py`, `presets.gps_1999` |",
    "| A20 | **FAA coverage method as reproduced** | 5 deg grid (2,376 points, 80S-80N), every minute for 24 h, 5 deg mask, good = 4+ satellites and PDOP <= 6; "
    "receivers on our sphere (the FAA presumably used the WGS-84 ellipsoid). The report does not say which day of each week was used: we use the 24 h "
    "from each almanac's reference time. It does not define 'global 99.9% PDOP' either: the mean over grid points of each point's own 99.9% PDOP "
    "reproduces its values, while pooling all point-minutes comes out about 0.8 higher; this definition is inferred from the data | `faa.py` |",
]
s = "\n".join(lines)

sub("| 2026-10-31 | **A6 changed, A18 added**",
    "| 2026-10-31 | **A19, A20 added** (Stage 5): real 1999 GPS orbits from almanacs, and the FAA's coverage method | To reproduce a published result "
    "(FAA Report #26, Table 2-1) with the satellites actually in orbit, and to compare it with our idealized Walker 24/6/1. See 'Comparison with "
    "published data' below. |\n| 2026-10-31 | **A6 changed, A18 added**")

data = json.loads(pathlib.Path("web/data/faa_reproduction.json").read_text())
rows = []
for w in data["weeks"]:
    pub, r = w["published"], w["real"]
    note = ""
    if "explanation" in w:
        x = w["explanation"]["result"]
        note = (f"with {w['explanation']['label']}: {x['global_999_pdop']:.2f} / {x['global_average_pct']:.3f} / {x['worst_point_pct']:.3f}"
                if w["week"] != 1007 else "not explained (see below)")
    rows.append(f"| {w['week']} | {pub['global_999_pdop']:.2f} / {pub['global_average_pct']:.3f} / {pub['worst_point_pct']:.3f} | "
                f"{r['global_999_pdop']:.2f} / {r['global_average_pct']:.3f} / {r['worst_point_pct']:.3f} | {note} |")
ideal = data["ideal"]
section = f"""## Comparison with published data (Stage 5)

**FAA GPS SPS Performance Analysis Report #26 (1999), Table 2-1** gives, for GPS weeks 1003-1016, the global 99.9%
PDOP, the global average availability and the worst-case point (see A20 for the method). We recomputed every week
with the same weekly almanacs (`tools/reproduce_faa.py`, about 7 minutes; the Compare tab shows the stored results
and can recompute any week in the browser, about 3 minutes):

| Week | FAA: 99.9% PDOP / global % / worst % | Ours, real almanac (healthy satellites) | Another satellite set |
|---|---|---|---|
""" + "\n".join(rows) + f"""

Our ideal Walker 24/6/1 by the same method: {ideal['global_999_pdop']:.2f} / {ideal['global_average_pct']:.3f} / {ideal['worst_point_pct']:.3f}, better
than the real 1999 constellation in every week, although the real one had 27 satellites: the evenly spaced slots
matter more than the extra satellites.

What this shows:
- **9 weeks match with no adjustment** (99.9% PDOP within 0.02-0.05; the availabilities exactly, in 1003-1006,
  1013 and 1015 to all three published decimals; in 1008-1011 the worst point differs by one minute of 1,440).
- **Weeks 1012, 1014 and 1016 match once the satellite set does**: the FAA evidently kept PRN 15 in week 1012 and
  only left out PRN 15 (not PRN 16 or PRN 9) in weeks 1014 and 1016, although the CelesTrak copies of those almanacs
  flag more satellites. Almanacs are reissued within a week and health flags change, so this is plausible, but it is
  an inference: the report does not list the satellites it used.
- **Week 1007 is not explained.** The FAA reports a 99.9% PDOP of 5.02 and a worst point of 98.264%; with every
  satellite in the almanac we get 3.23 and 99.931%, and leaving out any one of PRN 7, 9, 15 or 16 does not come
  close. A satellite outage during the FAA's (unknown) day, or a different day, would explain it; the report's own
  text says the highest contour for that week was "between 4 and 5". This difference is reported, not forced.

**Langley (1999)**: his worked DOP values are reproduced to all published decimals (GDOP 1.581 and 1.732; HDOP 1.195
and VDOP 1.558 with one satellite at the zenith and three at 15 deg; VDOP 0.913 when the clock is known). The
highest elevation of an ideal GPS satellite seen from the pole is 45.3 deg ("about 45"). For Fredericton with a 5 deg
mask over one day (week 1007 almanac) we get a mean GDOP of 1.98 and a maximum of 3.43 (Figure 5: "about two",
"never exceeds 3.5").

"""
sub("## Data and sources\n", section + "## Data and sources\n")
sub("- Monte Carlo: the vectorized batch agrees with the scalar calculation,",
    "- Stage 5: the almanac parser against the file text, almanac orbits (radius, latitude, period, ground-track repeat, the "
    "ascending node where IS-GPS-200 says), the GPS 1999 preset placing satellites exactly where the almanac does, the FAA grid, "
    "the stored reproduction against Table 2-1 in the weeks whose satellite set is not in doubt, the recompute path, and Langley's values;\n"
    "- Monte Carlo: the vectorized batch agrees with the scalar calculation,")
p.write_text(s); print("README updated")
EOF
grep -n "^## " README.md

content.text:
Stage 5 is built and checked against the published data. All 211 Python tests and all eight browser suites pass, with no JavaScript errors. It isn't committed yet.

## The headline result: reproducing the FAA's 1999 Table 2-1

I downloaded the **same 14 weekly almanacs the FAA used** (GPS weeks 1003–1016, from CelesTrak) and implemented the standard GPS almanac orbit algorithm, IS-GPS-200. I then recomputed the table the FAA's way: a 5° grid of 2,376 points, every minute for 24 hours, a 5° mask, and "good" meaning 4+ satellites and PDOP ≤ 6.

- **10 of 14 weeks match with no adjustment.** In weeks 1003–1006, 1013 and 1015 the availabilities match to all three published decimals. The 99.9% PDOP is within 0.01–0.05 in all ten.
- **Weeks 1012, 1014 and 1016 match once the satellite set does.** The FAA evidently kept PRN 15 in 1012 and left out only PRN 15 in 1014 and 1016, although the downloaded almanacs flag more satellites. That's an inference: the report doesn't list its satellites.
- **Week 1007 is not explained.** The FAA reports 5.02; we get 3.23. Removing any one of PRN 7, 9, 15 or 16 doesn't come close; I didn't try every satellite. I report it as an open difference rather than forcing it.
- **Ideal Walker 24/6/1:** 3.14 / 100% / 100%. That's better than the real 27-satellite 1999 constellation in every week, so the even spacing matters more than the extra satellites.

## A finding you should know about

The report never defines "global 99.9% PDOP". My first reading, pooling all point-minutes, was about 0.8 too high in every week. I then tested other definitions: **"the average over grid points of each point's own 99.9% PDOP"** reproduces the published values (3.30 vs 3.31, 3.70 vs 3.71, and so on). The app and README show both and label this definition as *inferred*. It's a good example of checking a model against data, which you may want to mention in your write-up.

## Langley (1999)

All six of his worked DOP values match to every published decimal, including VDOP 0.913 with the clock known. That needed a new "known clock" option in the DOP code. The pole's highest elevation is 45.3° ("about 45"). For Fredericton on one 1999 day, mean GDOP is 1.98 and the maximum 3.43, against his "about two" and "never exceeds 3.5".

## What's in the app

- **Compare tab:**
  - A metric selector, a chart with three series, and a week-by-week table with the differences.
  - Click a week for details, including the satellite-set explanation.
  - Langley's checks with ✓.
  - **"Recompute this week"**, which reruns a week in the browser and reports whether it matches the stored result. It works and matched exactly, but it takes **about 3 minutes** in browser Python.
- **PDOP map toggle:** colours each 5° cell on the globe by the PDOP met 99.99% of the time, for a chosen week or the ideal model. The cells turn with the Earth.
- **GPS 1999 preset:** a card with the 27 real satellites. Set the date to 1999-05-01 to see them where they actually were.
- **BeiDou:** your `paper/beidou.pdf` turned out to be the official ICD. It **confirms** our BeiDou parameters, and `papers.txt` now says "verified".

## Things to know

- **Repository size:** the almanacs and results add 436 KB under `web/data/`.
- **My own mistakes this round:**
  - Some test expectations were wrong; I fixed the tests, not the code.
  - My server cleanup command killed itself once.
  - I miscounted the matching weeks in a README draft (9 instead of 10) and caught it before it shipped.
- **README:** A19 (the almanac model) and A20 (the FAA method, including the inferred definition) are new, with a change-log entry and a results section.

Shall I commit and push?

message.content: Add a loading screen so it doesn't feel like it's not working at the start. Add the moon and the sun into the background and make the moon revolve around the Earth. Make sure their orbits are realistic. Make the lighting reflect the sun's position. Remove the rounded corners from the UI.

content.text: I'll check the technical choices with you first. "Realistic" can mean a few different things here, and one choice affects how the whole scene looks.

questions.question: How should the Moon's distance and size be shown? At true scale it orbits 60 Earth radii away (384,400 km), 15 times farther than GPS, and is about a quarter of the Earth's size.

options.label: True distance and size, zoom out to see it (Recommended)
options.description: Moon at its real, varying distance (356,000-407,000 km) and real radius (1,737 km). The default view stays on the Earth and satellites; you scroll out (max zoom raised to ~150 Earth radii) to see the Moon go round. Physically honest.

options.label: True direction, distance compressed
options.description: Moon in its true direction but drawn closer (e.g. 12 Earth radii) so it is always in view. Its orbit shape is real but scaled; looks nicer, but distances are wrong.

questions.question: How should the Sun be shown?

options.label: Glowing disc far in the background, true direction (Recommended)
options.description: A bright sun disc with a soft glow placed far away in its true direction (its true distance is 23,500 Earth radii, too far to draw); drawn somewhat larger than its true 0.5 deg so it is visible. Its light comes from that direction.

options.label: Light only, no visible sun
options.description: Only the lighting follows the Sun; nothing is drawn.

questions.question: How realistic should the day/night lighting on the Earth be?

options.label: Clear day/night, night side dim but visible (Recommended)
options.description: Sunlit side bright, night side darkened to about 25% so continents are still recognisable. The Moon shows its real phase because it is lit by the same Sun.

options.label: Physically dark night side
options.description: Night side almost black, like a real photo. Dramatic, but half the globe becomes hard to read (clicking it still works).

questions.question: How precise should the Sun and Moon positions be? Both come from standard astronomical formulas (Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, the same book as our sidereal time), checked against his worked examples.

options.label: Good: Sun to ~0.01 deg, Moon to ~0.3 deg (Recommended)
options.description: Short series (about 10 lines each). Far below what you can see on screen; easy to read and check against Meeus's examples.

options.label: High: Moon with Meeus's full ~60-term series (~0.003 deg)
options.description: Longer table of coefficients to type in and check; no visible difference in the app.
